network.overall_strategy: This synthesis network integrates both Strecker-nitrile and α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) metabolic-analog routes, reflecting the dual families of prebiotic glutamate synthesis identified in the literature. It explicitly includes C4 precursor bottlenecks (3-cyanopropanal and α-KG), nitrene/nitrile channels (via cyanosulfidic photochemistry and atmospheric discharge/Spark-Strecker), protometabolic Fe-catalyzed routes, Bucherer–Bergs hydantoin chemistry, and hydrothermal thermodynamic routes. Parallel modular feeder pathways converge at aminonitrile, α-KG, and hydantoin nodes, allowing for a diverse array of plausible geochemical scenarios. Pyroglutamate—the cyclization product of glutamate—is incorporated as a reversible reservoir node. All ten pathways ultimately deliver glutamate under non-enzymatic, prebiotic, iron-rich, anoxic conditions, in accord with geochemical and meteoritic constraints.

reactions.name: Conjugate addition of HCN to acrolein
reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of HCN to the β position of acrolein yields 3-cyanopropanal.
reactions.reasoning: This step is proposed based on the mechanism outlined in Van Trump & Miller (1972) and supported by Parker et al. (2011) as plausible for prebiotic settings; however, explicit glutamate yields remain undemonstrated for this sequence.

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis of aminonitrile from 3-cyanopropanal

conditions.other: alkaline to neutral pH; classic Strecker aqueous conditions

reactions.mechanism: Amination and cyanide addition to the aldehyde to form the α-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Standard Strecker-type chemistry demonstrated robustly for other amino acids, plausible for this substrate (Johnson et al. 2008; Cleaves et al. 2008).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of 2-aminopentanedinitrile to glutamine and/or glutamate
reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydrolysis/subsequent amide formation to yield glutamine, which may hydrolyze further to glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Analogous nitrile hydrolysis is established in acid/base-catalyzed prebiotic aqueous chemistry (Patel et al. 2015). Complete hydrolysis is slow but plausible on wet-dry minerals.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of glutamine to glutamate
reactions.mechanism: Amide hydrolysis on mineral or in solution yields glutamate from glutamine.
reactions.reasoning: Glutamine hydrolysis to glutamate is a key and chemically simple step, known to proceed in model systems (see cyanosulfidic schemes: Patel et al. 2015).

reactions.name: Photoreduction of cyanoacetylene to succinonitrile (cyanosulfidic photochemistry)
reactions.mechanism: UV-assisted photoreduction of cyanoacetylene (with H2S) to the C4 dinitrile via copper-catalyzed redox photochemistry.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) demonstrated this sequence experimentally, including the step yielding succinonitrile as a C4 skeleton precursor.

reactions.name: Photoreduction of succinonitrile to 3-cyanopropanal
reactions.mechanism: Selective reduction of one nitrile to an aldehyde, yielding 3-cyanopropanal.
reactions.reasoning: An experimentally supported photoreduction in the Patel et al. (2015) cyanosulfidic network.

reactions.name: Glyoxylate–pyruvate condensation to hydroxyketoglutarate/oxopentenedioate and reduction to α-ketoglutarate

conditions.other: neutral to mildly alkaline; can occur both with and without metal

reactions.mechanism: Aldol addition followed by rearrangement and reduction yields α-ketoglutarate.
reactions.reasoning: Metal-catalyzed and metal-free α-KG formation from glyoxylate and pyruvate is robust (Muchowska et al. 2019; Stubbs et al. 2020).

reactions.name: Reductive amination of α-ketoglutarate to glutamate (FeS, H2 or Ni/H2/HCO3)

conditions.other: NH4+ or NH3 present; moderately alkaline

reactions.mechanism: Reductive amination of the ketoacid yields glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Nonenzymatic FeS- and Ni/H2-driven reductive amination established under hydrothermal and vent-analogue conditions (Huber & Wächtershäuser 2003; Kitadai et al. 2019; Kaur et al. 2024).

reactions.name: Bucherer–Bergs hydantoin formation from α-ketoglutarate

conditions.other: DAP or NH3 as N-source; neutral to mildly basic

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide and ammonia react with α-KG to form glutamate hydantoin.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated prebiotic hydantoin formation on α-ketoacids with subsequent glutamate release; yields for hydantoin are high, but Glu is partial (Pulletikurti et al. 2022).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of glutamate hydantoin to glutamate

conditions.other: acidic or basic hydrolysis, wet-dry cycles increase rate

reactions.mechanism: Ring opening of hydantoin and hydrolysis generates glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated experimentally with glutamate yield ~19% from hydantoin (Pulletikurti et al. 2022); high stability/reservoir for eventual release.

reactions.name: Nonenzymatic transamination: glycine + α-ketoglutarate

conditions.other: phosphate buffer or mineral surface; neutral pH

reactions.mechanism: Amino group transfer from glycine to α-KG yields glutamate; nonenzymatic exchange.
reactions.reasoning: Metal-free transamination is robust for α-ketoacids (Stubbs et al. 2020); no catalyst required.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of HCN oligomers yields glutamate

conditions.other: strong acid/base hydrolysis, requires history of HCN concentration

reactions.mechanism: Random breaking of HCN oligomers releases various amino acids including glutamate upon hydrolysis.
reactions.reasoning: Ruiz-Bermejo et al. (2013) and previous studies establish this as a generic but very inefficient source of glutamate.

reactions.name: Cyclization of glutamate to pyroglutamic acid

conditions.other: promoted by low pH, wet-dry cycles, or thermally

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular cyclization of glutamate via the amino group to the gamma-carboxyl, forming a 5-membered ring.
reactions.reasoning: Well-documented prebiotic side-reaction and reservoir; seen in meteorites and laboratory decompositions (Gayte-Sorbier et al.; Wu et al. 2010).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of pyroglutamate to glutamate

conditions.other: acidic or basic hydrolysis, wet-dry cycles

reactions.mechanism: Ring opening under hydrolysis conditions restores glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Observed in acid hydrolysis of meteorite extracts (Pizzarello & Cooper 2001). Pyroglutamate can thus act as a dynamic prebiotic reservoir of Glu.

reactions.name: Hydrothermal direct reduction of CO2 to glutamate
reactions.mechanism: Overall net reduction and amination of CO2 and NH3 to glutamate under reducing, Fe-rich hydrothermal vent conditions.
reactions.reasoning: Supported thermodynamically by Amend & Shock (1998), though strongly critiqued for lack of kinetic evidence (Bada & Miller 1995; Aubrey et al. 2009).

pathways.name: Spark-acrolein Strecker pathway
pathways.description: HCN from electric discharge chemistry combines with acrolein to give 3-cyanopropanal, which undergoes Strecker synthesis to aminonitrile and then hydrolysis to glutamate via glutamine.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic photochemical nitrile pathway
pathways.description: Cyanoacetylene undergoes repeated photoreduction with H2S and UV, forming succinonitrile and then 3-cyanopropanal. Entry into the Strecker sequence leads to glutamate.

pathways.name: α-Ketoglutarate metabolic analogue pathway
pathways.description: Glyoxylate and pyruvate condense (FeII/phosphate mineral catalysis) to α-ketoglutarate, then undergo reductive amination to glutamate under FeS or Ni/H2 conditions.

pathways.name: Bucherer–Bergs hydantoin pathway on α-KG
pathways.description: α-Ketoglutarate reacts with NH3 and HCN to form glutamate hydantoin, which hydrolyzes to glutamate. This provides a bridge between nitrile and metabolic routes.

pathways.name: Nonenzymatic glycine transamination pathway
pathways.description: Glyoxylate + pyruvate furnish α-KG, which then undergoes transamination with glycine to form glutamate.

pathways.name: HCN oligomer hydrolysis pathway
pathways.description: Concentrated HCN polymerizes under evaporitic/surface conditions; subsequent hydrolysis liberates glutamate.

pathways.name: Pyroglutamate hydroplay
pathways.description: Any pathway that reaches free glutamate also enables cyclization to pyroglutamate and subsequent hydrolysis back, serving as a reservoir and sink for Glu under evaporative and hydrothermal fluctuations.

pathways.name: Direct hydrothermal reduction pathway
pathways.description: Reduction and amination of CO2/NH3 in Fe-rich hydrothermal systems yield glutamate directly (theoretically favorable thermodynamics, debated kinetics).

pathways.name: Photochemical C4 nitrile reservoir branch
pathways.description: Cyanoacetylene and H2S photoreduction produces succinonitrile and then 3-cyanopropanal, which can feed directly into the Bucherer–Bergs condensation or aminonitrile formation.

pathways.name: Meteoritic/extraterrestrial delivery pathway
pathways.description: Glutamate, pyroglutamate, and their hydrolysis/condensation products can be delivered by meteorites, with hydrolysis releasing free glutamate in surface/evaporitic environments.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The acrolein Strecker pathway (P1) closely tracks the originally proposed Miller-Van Trump route, but all steps (except the first) are mass-imbalanced as shown by the atom balance check. The Strecker sequence is plausible, but the overall pathway fails conservation on several reactions. No reported yields for the full sequence exist, and acrolein's conversion to glutamate has never been demonstrated experimentally. Correct stoichiometries (e.g., explicit H2O for hydrolyses) are missing, and some steps likely need additional ammonolysis or hydrolysis agents to be balanced. Correction required on rxn_002, rxn_003, and rxn_004.
suggestions: Add missing byproducts (likely H2O and/or NH3) to balance mass in hydrolysis and Strecker steps.
Provide explicit stoichiometry or cite literature with full balances.
If hypothesizing this path, flag all but the first step as 'proposed/unconfirmed'.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The cyanosulfidic photochemical C4 nitrile pathway (P2) is conceptually well-aligned with Patel et al. (2015) but nearly all reactions are severely unbalanced (rxn_005, rxn_006, rxn_002, rxn_003, rxn_004). Mechanistically, the C4 intermediates and photoreductions are plausible, but atom counts fail, indicating major stoichiometric omissions. Hydrolysis and reductive steps are under-specified. Surface/UV conditions are plausible, but Cu(I)/Cu(II) and H2S requirements should be explicit if matching Sutherland conditions.
suggestions: Add balancing species (H2, H2O, NH3, S-product) per mechanistic requirements in all photoreduction and hydrolytic steps.
Clarify need for Cu photoredox if following literature.
Explicitly cite and match stoichiometries from Supplementary Info (Patel et al. 2015), or else indicate proposed-only steps.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This α-ketoglutarate metabolic-analogue route follows the best-supported experimental prebiotic chemistry (glyoxylate/pyruvate + Fe2+, then reductive amination of α-KG). However, both steps are unbalanced (rxn_007 needs CO2 or O2 byproducts, rxn_008 is off by H2O/O); mass/charge are not conserved as written. Mechanistically, these are real, and conditions (70°C, Fe2+, pH ~7–9) are correct per Muchowska 2019 and Kitadai 2019. Target achievement is upheld only if balances are corrected.
suggestions: Show the missing byproducts on condensation (CO2 loss, explicit H2O formation on amination).
Adopt explicit stoichiometries from primary sources.
If using FeS or H2/Ni, state required conditions in network legend.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Bucherer–Bergs α-KG/hydantoin path mirrors recent advances but is entirely unbalanced (rxn_009, rxn_010, and dependent rxn_004), with atom/charge errors unfixable by adding typical small molecules. The concept is literature-backed (Pulletikurti 2022), but hydrolysis and condensation require explicit balancing species. Cyanide and DAP reagent plausibility should be noted.
suggestions: Add known byproducts (e.g., H2O, CO2, NH3) per hydrolysis and hydantoin equilibria.
Show cyanide/DAP requirements up front.
Cite explicit yields from Pulletikurti et al. if possible, and update reaction balances for network consistency.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Glycine transamination is valid nonenzymatic chemistry (Stubbs 2020, Kaur 2024), but both reactions fail mass balance; rxn_011 especially (transamination) is off by C, H, and O, so stoichiometry must include formaldehyde or other compensating byproducts. Environmental fit is good. Only approved if full balances are shown.
suggestions: Add full stoichiometry (e.g., show pyruvate/glyoxylate transamination gives a reciprocal α-ketoacid/amino acid pair with possibly swapped carbon skeletons).
Provide explicit byproducts (e.g. glyoxylate/alanine etc.)
Cite nonenzymatic transamination conditions explicitly.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The HCN oligomer hydrolysis route is not mass-balanced (C and H severely off), reflecting the fact that a direct HCN → Glu yield is not a mechanistically plausible step—rather, this encompasses a series of condensations, aminonitrile formation, and harsh hydrolysis as one node. Unless the polymer structure and hydrolysis stoichiometry are detailed, this is not a valid chemical step.
suggestions: Treat HCN polymerization and hydrolysis as multiple steps, with generic macromolecule and explicit H2O/NH3 evolution.
Only cite this route as a source of trace/racemic Glu after polymer analysis and hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyclization to pyroglutamate (rxn_013) is generally plausible with water loss, but the back hydrolysis (rxn_014) is unbalanced and does not adequately specify the need for harsh or catalytic conditions (acidic pH, high temp). This pathway can reasonably serve as a reversible reservoir, but only when balances are explicit.
suggestions: Balance water loss in cyclization and water/ammonia uptake in hydrolysis.
Cite conditions from Gayte-Sorbier et al. (pH, temperature).
Include rate constants if proposing reversibility.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This single-step, direct hydrothermal CO2/NH3 → Glu route is not chemically valid as written: it lacks any plausible mechanism for the multicarbon and multistep transformations required, fails mass conservation, and is only supported in literature as a one-step thermodynamic analysis (Amend & Shock 1998) with strong kinetic and stability objections. Not experimentally validated.
suggestions: Omit or replace with stepwise, literature-backed chemistry for C–C and CN bond formation.
Only reference as a thermodynamic driver, not as a real pathway.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Malformed pathway—rxn_016 is not defined in the reactions list (likely a typo), so the first step cannot be evaluated; the rest are severely unbalanced as above. Network connectivity and chemistry are unclear. Not valid as written.
suggestions: Define rxn_016 or correct to actual photoreduction/condensation sequence.
Verify all reaction balances and connectivities.
Remove undefined or placeholder steps.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Meteorite delivery is not a chemical synthesis pathway but a source term; while glutamate is indeed found as racemate in Bennu, this does not represent a stepwise chemical route and shares the non-conservation issues of rxn_012. Include as a boundary condition, not as a pathway.
suggestions: Clarify that exogenous delivery is not part of networked prebiotic chemistry.
Use as input (feedstock node) if appropriate.

evaluation.network_feedback: This synthesis network integrates all known major families of plausible prebiotic glutamate synthesis and models appropriate hubs and environmental branches in line with recent literature. However, nearly every reaction except the initial acrolein/HCN addition (rxn_001) fails deterministic atom and charge balance as checked programmatically. These mass conservation errors are not minor: they reflect missing byproducts (H2O, CO2, NH3, S-compounds, small organic acids) in essentially every hydrolysis, reduction, or C–C bond forming step, and cannot be fixed by adding a few extra H2O or CO2. The network's overall logic, topology, and environmental framing are excellent and literature-aligned (including explicit C4 bottlenecks and congruent prebiotic scenarios), but the execution falls short of approval due to stoichiometrically invalid transformations. To be viable, each reaction must have its mass and charge balance explicitly presented, using full experimental or literature stoichiometry. Literature evidence is robust for every module, and the role of pyroglutamate as a reversible sink is correctly included. Once reaction balances are rectified, and undefined/placeholder steps removed (e.g., rxn_016), this network would likely reach approval.
